title_options: Why A Hotter Pan Makes Water Last Longer (Leidenfrost Effect) 💧

share.myth: A hotter surface always makes water boil away faster.
share.truth: Above about 180 C, the bottom of a water drop vaporises so fast that it floats on a vapour film about 50 micrometres thick; vapour conducts heat poorly, so the drop evaporates more slowly and slides with almost no friction (Quéré 2013; Biance, Clanet & Quéré 2003).
share.line: Past about 180 degrees, steam becomes an insulator under the drop, so a hotter pan makes water last longer.

facts: Quéré 2013, Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics 45:197: Leidenfrost drops levitate on vapour injected beneath them; with no solid contact they are highly mobile.
Lagubeau, Le Merrer, Clanet & Quéré, APS DFD 2008: for water above about 180 C; vapour film about 50 micrometres.
Biance, Clanet & Quéré 2003, Physics of Fluids 15:1632: levitating drops evaporate slowly because heat must cross the vapour film; vapour has a low thermal conductivity.
description: Heat transfer, insulation and friction in one drop of water: why water skates on a very hot pan and lasts longer than on a warm one. #shorts #physics #science #heattransfer
sources: Quéré 2013, Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics 45:197; Biance, Clanet & Quéré 2003, Physics of Fluids 15:1632; Lagubeau et al., APS Division of Fluid Dynamics 2008.

scenes.narration: On a warm pan, water sizzles away. On a much hotter pan, it skates around and lasts longer.
That sounds backwards. More heat should mean faster boiling.
But above about one hundred eighty degrees Celsius, the bottom of the drop vaporises instantly.
That vapour forms a film about fifty micrometres thick, roughly the width of a hair.
With a gas film underneath, there's almost no contact, so almost no friction.
And gases are poor conductors of heat, so the film insulates the drop from the pan.
Heat has to cross that insulating layer, so the drop evaporates more slowly. That's the Leidenfrost effect.
Past about one hundred eighty degrees, steam becomes an insulator under the drop, so a hotter pan makes water last longer.
So why does a drop touching a cooler pan get heat so much faster?
